why_how.text: Your eyes and ears catch the hazards you must react to, so anything that blocks or dulls them makes driving riskier.
A medication you do not understand can make you unsafe without warning.

scenario.text: Jae plans to drive with earbuds in both ears and after taking a new over-the-counter allergy pill.

reasoning.text: Wearing a headset or earplugs in both ears is illegal, and over-the-counter drugs can make a driver unsafe, sometimes through sleepiness.

result.text: Jae removes the earbuds and learns the pill's effects before deciding whether to drive.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking over-the-counter medicine cannot affect driving.

correction.text: Prescription and over-the-counter drugs can both make a driver unsafe, so learn every medication's effects.

memory_support.text: Eyes open, ears open, know your meds.

prompt.text: Is it legal to drive wearing earplugs in both ears?

answer.text: No, wearing a headset or earplugs in both ears is illegal.

rationale.text: Drivers must hear horns, sirens, motorcycles and screeching tires, so both ears must stay uncovered.

lines.text: Your eyes and ears do the work.

narration.text: This lesson begins the introduction to driving by looking at you, the driver. Safe driving depends on your eyes and ears picking up what is happening around you, and on your body and mind being ready to react. We will look at what driving vision involves, what you must be able to hear, and why covering both ears is illegal. Then we will look at fatigue, medications, and the rule that physicians must report certain medical conditions. By the end you will have a simple checklist for whether you are ready to drive before you ever turn the key.

Driving vision is more than seeing the road. It means spotting hazards as the light changes, judging gaps between vehicles, matching the speed of traffic, and reading signs. Each of those is a separate job your eyes must do at the same time. Fatigue and drowsiness degrade your vision and slow your reactions to hazards, so a tired driver loses some of each of these skills. You also need to stay alert enough to pick the right move quickly in every traffic situation, including surprises. Clear vision and steady alertness work together to keep you ahead of trouble.

Your ears are a second set of eyes on the road. Drivers must be able to hear horns, sirens, motorcycles, and screeching tires, because those sounds often warn of danger before you can see it. That is why wearing a headset or earplugs in both ears while driving is illegal. Eyes and ears work as a team: eyes judge light, gaps, speed, and signs, while ears track horns, sirens, bikes, and skids, and both ears must stay uncovered. If something blocks your hearing, you lose warnings that could give you the time you need to react safely.

Three things can make an otherwise capable driver unsafe. Fatigue and drowsiness degrade vision and slow reactions. Prescription and over-the-counter drugs can make a driver unsafe, sometimes by causing sleepiness, so you should learn the effects of every medication you take. And physicians must report patients aged fourteen and up whose medical conditions, such as a lapse of consciousness, could impair safe driving. Put together, tiredness dulls your senses and speed, medications can sedate or impair you, and doctors must report risky conditions from age fourteen. Each one is a reason to check yourself before driving.

Here is a trap. Many people assume that a medicine bought without a prescription cannot affect their driving. The handbook says otherwise: prescription and over-the-counter drugs can both make a driver unsafe, sometimes through sleepiness. That is why you should learn every medication's effects before you drive. A second trap is the idea that earbuds are fine if the music is quiet. Wearing a headset or earplugs in both ears is illegal, whatever the volume. In both cases the rule protects your senses: you need clear eyes, open ears, and an alert mind behind the wheel.

Here is a quick check: is it legal to drive while wearing earplugs in both ears? Settle on your answer. The answer is no. Wearing a headset or earplugs in both ears while driving is illegal. Drivers must be able to hear horns, sirens, motorcycles, and screeching tires, and those sounds often warn of danger before you can see it. If you answered no, you have the hearing rule. If you hesitated, remember the pairing from this lesson: eyes judge light, gaps, speed, and signs, ears track horns and sirens, and both ears must stay uncovered.

To sum up, driving vision means spotting hazards in changing light, judging gaps, matching traffic speed, and reading signs. You must be able to hear horns, sirens, motorcycles, and screeching tires, and wearing a headset or earplugs in both ears is illegal. Fatigue and drowsiness degrade vision and slow reactions, and prescription or over-the-counter drugs can make you unsafe, so learn each medication's effects. Physicians must report patients aged fourteen and up with conditions that could impair driving. Stay alert enough to choose the right move fast. Next we look at how to hold and turn the steering wheel.

why_how.text: The right steering method keeps the vehicle under control in each kind of turn.
Knowing when one hand is enough keeps both hands on the wheel the rest of the time.

scenario.text: Lia is backing out of a driveway and needs to turn around to watch behind her.

reasoning.text: One hand suffices when turning while backing to watch behind, with that hand at the twelve o'clock spot.

result.text: Lia places one hand at twelve o'clock and turns to look behind as she backs slowly.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking push-pull steering lets your hands cross over the center of the wheel.

correction.text: Push-pull never crosses hands past the wheel's center and holds the nine and three or eight and four spots through turns.

memory_support.text: Push-pull never crosses; hand-over-hand is for slow turns.

prompt.text: Where does your hand go when you steer with one hand while backing?

answer.text: At the twelve o'clock spot on the wheel.

rationale.text: Backing while watching behind is one of only two one-hand cases, and the hand sits at twelve o'clock.

narration.text: This lesson is about steering. How you hold and turn the wheel affects how well you control the vehicle, especially in turns and emergencies. The default is simple: keep both hands on the wheel whenever possible. From there, the handbook describes two steering methods, push-pull and hand-over-hand, each suited to different situations, and two cases in which one hand is enough. We will cover the hand positions for each method, the step-by-step hand-over-hand sequence, and when you may drop to one hand. Practice these until they feel natural before you drive in traffic.

lines.text: Start at nine and three or eight and four.

narration.text: Push-pull steering is a hand-to-hand method. Your hands start at the nine and three o'clock positions or the eight and four o'clock positions. As you turn, one hand pushes the wheel up while the other pulls, and your hands never cross past the center of the wheel. They hold those spots through the whole turn. This method keeps both hands planted, which is the default rule: both hands stay on the wheel, and push-pull keeps them at nine-three or eight-four without ever crossing the center. That gives you steady control through ordinary turns.

Hand-over-hand steering fits three situations: low-speed turns, parking, and recovering from a skid. These are the times when crossing your arms is allowed. Hand-over-hand is different from push-pull because your arms do cross. It is not for every turn. At normal speeds, push-pull keeps your hands from crossing. When you are turning slowly, maneuvering into a parking space, or correcting a skid, hand-over-hand lets you turn the wheel further and faster. So the method you choose depends on the situation, and slow turns, parking, and skids are the cue for hand-over-hand.

lines.text: Reach across, release, reach over, pull up.

narration.text: Hand-over-hand follows a set sequence. Start with your hands at the eight and four o'clock positions. Reach across to the far side of the wheel with one hand. Release the other hand. Then reach across the gripping arm with the released hand and pull up. Repeating those steps turns the wheel smoothly. Notice the starting position: eight and four o'clock, which is also one of the push-pull starting positions. What makes hand-over-hand different is the reaching across, which is exactly what push-pull never does. Practice the sequence slowly in a parking lot first.

There are only two times when one hand on the wheel is enough. The first is when you are turning while backing and need to watch behind you; then your one hand goes at the twelve o'clock spot. The second is when you are working a control that forces a hand off the wheel. Outside those two cases, both hands stay on the wheel whenever possible. So the full picture is: cross arms only for slow turns, parking, and skid recovery, and drop to one hand only for backing at twelve o'clock or for forced control use. Those two cases are the whole list.

lines.text: Truth: crossing is only for hand-over-hand.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Because hand-over-hand crosses the arms, learners sometimes let their hands cross in push-pull steering too. Push-pull never crosses hands past the wheel's center, and it holds the nine and three or eight and four spots through turns. Crossing arms belongs only to hand-over-hand, used for low-speed turns, parking, and skid recovery. A second trap is driving with one hand on the wheel out of habit. One hand is enough only when backing with the hand at twelve o'clock or when working a control. The rest of the time, keep both hands on the wheel.

lines.text: Where does your one hand go?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: when you steer with one hand while backing and turning to watch behind you, where does that hand go? Decide first. The answer is the twelve o'clock spot. Backing while watching behind is one of only two cases where one hand is enough; the other is when a control forces a hand off the wheel. If you answered twelve o'clock, you have the backing rule. If not, picture the top of the wheel as the spot for one-hand backing, and keep both hands on the wheel at all other times whenever you can. Two hands is the habit to build.

lines.text: Hand-over-hand for slow turns and skids.

narration.text: To wrap up, keep both hands on the wheel whenever possible. Push-pull steering starts at nine and three or eight and four o'clock, never crosses the center, and holds those spots through turns. Hand-over-hand fits low-speed turns, parking, and skid recovery: start at eight and four, reach across to the far side, release the other hand, then reach across the gripping arm and pull up. One hand is enough only when backing with the hand at twelve o'clock or when working a control. Next, we look at how you communicate with other road users through signals.

why_how.text: Signals tell other drivers, pedestrians and bicyclists what you are about to do, so they can react in time.
Signaling at the right distance and time is a rule with exact numbers.

scenario.text: Omar is on the freeway and wants to move one lane to the left.

reasoning.text: You signal ahead of every lane change, and at least five seconds before a freeway lane change.

result.text: Omar signals for at least five seconds, changes lanes, then switches the signal off.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you can skip the signal when the road looks empty.

correction.text: You also signal on empty-looking roads, as well as for curb pull-ins and pull-outs and late turns just past an intersection.

memory_support.text: Feet for turns, seconds on freeways, then cancel.

prompt.text: How long before a freeway lane change must you signal?

rationale.text: Freeway lane changes need at least five seconds of signal, while turns need at least one hundred feet.

narration.text: This lesson is about signaling. Your signals, horn, and headlights are how you speak to other drivers, pedestrians, and bicyclists. In this lesson we focus on signals: which moves you must signal, when to use hand-and-arm signals instead of lamps, how a bicyclist signals a turn, and the exact distances and times the handbook sets for signaling. We will also cover a few situations people forget to signal and the simple rule about switching the signal off. These rules come with numbers, so we will practice telling them apart so they do not get mixed up later.

You must signal every turn, lane change, slowdown, and stop. You can signal with your signal lamps or with hand-and-arm positions. Use arm signals when the lamps fail or when harsh sun hides them, so other drivers can still see what you intend. Bicyclists signal too: a bicyclist may mark a turn by extending one arm straight toward that side. So drivers signal moves four ways, with lamps or arms, and cyclists answer with one straight arm toward the turn. Watching for those straight-arm signals helps you predict what a bicyclist ahead of you is about to do.

lines.text: At least one hundred feet before a turn.
Five seconds before a freeway lane change.

narration.text: The handbook sets exact signaling rules. Signal at least one hundred feet before a turn. Signal ahead of every lane change. And signal at least five seconds before a freeway lane change. Notice that one rule uses distance and the other uses time: one hundred feet for turns, five seconds for freeway lane changes. Keep them paired that way. Signaling early gives other road users time to react before you move. Once the signal has served its purpose, switch it off, so it does not keep telling other drivers you are about to turn when you are not.

lines.text: Pulling in or out at a curb.

narration.text: Some signals are easy to forget. You must also signal when pulling in to or out from a curb. You must signal even on roads that look empty, because someone you have not noticed may be relying on your signal. And you must signal for a turn that comes right after you pass through an intersection, signaling late, once you are through the intersection, so drivers there are not misled. The full set of signal rules then reads: one hundred feet for turns, five seconds for freeway lane changes, plus curbs, empty roads, and late intersection turns, then cancel.

lines.text: Trap: no one around, no signal needed.
Truth: signal on empty-looking roads too.

narration.text: Here is a trap. When the road looks empty, many drivers skip the signal because there seems to be no one to tell. The handbook says to signal on empty-looking roads too. A second trap is mixing up the numbers: some drivers signal five seconds before a turn and one hundred feet before a freeway lane change. That swaps the rules. Turns need at least one hundred feet of signal, and freeway lane changes need at least five seconds. A third trap is leaving the signal on after the move. Switch it off once it has served its purpose.

Here is a quick check: how long before a freeway lane change must you signal? Choose your answer. The answer is at least five seconds. That is the freeway lane change rule, measured in time. Turns follow a different rule, measured in distance: at least one hundred feet before the turn. If you answered five seconds, you have the pair right. If you answered one hundred feet, you swapped the two rules, so tie seconds to the freeway and feet to turns. Either way, switch the signal off once the move is done. Seconds belong to the freeway.

lines.text: Signal every move, lamps or arms.
Feet for turns, seconds on freeways.

narration.text: To wrap up, signals, horn, and headlights speak to drivers, pedestrians, and bicyclists. Signal every turn, lane change, slowdown, and stop with lamps or hand-and-arm positions, using arm signals when lamps fail or harsh sun hides them. Bicyclists may mark a turn with one arm straight toward that side. Signal at least one hundred feet before turns, ahead of every lane change, and at least five seconds before freeway lane changes. Also signal at curbs, on empty-looking roads, and for turns just past an intersection, then switch the signal off. Next, horn and headlights.

why_how.text: Using the horn and lights at the right moments lets others see and hear you, and keeps high beams from blinding them.

scenario.text: At night on a two-lane road, Ben has his high beams on when an oncoming car appears in the distance.

reasoning.text: You drop from high to low beams within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic and within three hundred feet behind a vehicle you follow.

result.text: Ben switches to low beams once the oncoming car is within five hundred feet.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking parking lights are enough when headlights are too bright.

correction.text: Driving with only parking lights is illegal; drop to low beams instead.

memory_support.text: Five hundred ahead, three hundred behind.

prompt.text: Within what distance of oncoming traffic must you switch from high to low beams?

rationale.text: High beams drop within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic and three hundred feet behind a followed vehicle.

lines.text: Headlights help you see and be seen.

narration.text: This lesson covers the horn and headlights, two more ways to communicate on the road. The horn lets you announce your presence or warn of danger. Headlights help you see and help others see you, but high beams can also blind other drivers if you do not dim them in time. We will look at when to sound the horn, the exact distances for dropping from high to low beams, the time window when headlights must be on because of darkness, and the many other conditions that call for low beams even in daylight. Several numbers appear here, so watch them closely.

lines.text: Narrow mountain roads with short sight.

narration.text: Sound the horn to announce your presence or to flag danger. Two uses are named: to help avert a collision, and to warn oncoming drivers on narrow mountain roads where you can see less than two hundred feet ahead. On those roads, a driver coming around a bend may not see you in time, so the horn gives them warning. The horn is for warnings, not for impatience. Pairing it with the next rule helps: horns warn of presence and danger on blind mountain bends, while high beams drop for oncoming and followed traffic at set distances.

lines.text: Within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic.
Within three hundred feet behind a vehicle.

narration.text: High beams light far ahead, but they can blind other drivers. Drop from high to low beams within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic, and within three hundred feet when you are following another vehicle. The two numbers are different because the situations are different: an oncoming car faces your lights head on, while a car ahead sees them in its mirrors. Do not switch to parking lights only, because driving with only parking lights is illegal. So the rule is to dim to low beams at those distances, never to drop down to parking lights.

lines.text: Weather, murk, mountains, tunnels, signs, low sun.

narration.text: Turn headlights on when darkness hides things beyond one thousand feet, from thirty minutes after sunset until thirty minutes before sunrise. Low beams are also needed in other conditions: in weather that calls for your wipers, in murk such as clouds, dust, smoke, or fog, on mountain roads and in tunnels even in sunshine, wherever signs require lights, and to help you stand out when the sun is low. So headlights answer the darkness clock and also weather, murk, mountains, signs, and low sun together. When in doubt in poor conditions, low beams help others see you.

lines.text: Trap: no lights needed in sunshine.
Truth: mountain roads and tunnels need them.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Drivers often think headlights are only for nighttime. But low beams are called for on mountain roads and in tunnels even in sunshine, in wiper weather, in murk such as fog or smoke, where signs require lights, and when low sun makes it hard to see you. A second trap is dimming too late, or dimming to parking lights. Drop to low beams within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic and three hundred feet behind a followed vehicle, and remember that driving on parking lights alone is illegal. Low beams, not parking lights.

Here is a quick check: within what distance of oncoming traffic must you switch from high to low beams? Pick your answer. The answer is within five hundred feet. When you are following another vehicle, the distance is three hundred feet behind it. If you answered five hundred feet, you have the oncoming rule. If you answered three hundred feet, you picked the following rule, so tie five hundred to oncoming traffic and three hundred to the car you follow. In both cases, drop to low beams, never to parking lights alone.

lines.text: Dim at set distances; lights on when needed.

narration.text: To wrap up, sound the horn to announce your presence or flag danger, including warning oncoming drivers on narrow mountain roads with less than two hundred feet of sight. Drop from high to low beams within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic and within three hundred feet behind a vehicle you follow, and never drive on parking lights alone. Turn headlights on from thirty minutes after sunset until thirty minutes before sunrise, when darkness hides things beyond one thousand feet, and use low beams for wiper weather, murk, mountain roads and tunnels, signed zones, and low sun.

why_how.text: Warning drivers behind you and stopping where you can be seen prevents a second crash.

scenario.text: Ana's car starts losing power on a two-lane road just past a curve.

reasoning.text: Trouble stops start with flashers and pulling fully off the road; if that is impossible, stop where drivers behind can see you, never just past a curve or hill crest.

result.text: Ana turns on her flashers, moves to a spot where drivers behind can see her clearly, pulls fully off the road, calls for help and waits inside.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should get out and walk for help after a breakdown.

correction.text: Call for roadside rescue and wait inside the vehicle until it comes.

memory_support.text: Warn behind, clear the road, wait inside.

prompt.text: You cannot get fully off the road. Where should you avoid stopping?

answer.text: Just past a hill crest or curve.

rationale.text: When fully clear is impossible, stop where drivers behind can see car and driver, never just past a crest or curve.

narration.text: This lesson covers what to do when something goes wrong on the road. There are two kinds of situations. In one, you see a hazard ahead and need to warn the drivers behind you as you slow down. In the other, your own vehicle has trouble and you need to stop safely. We will go through the three ways to warn drivers behind you, how to begin a trouble stop, where to stop if you cannot get fully off the road, and what to do while you wait for help. Each step is about being seen and staying out of the path of other traffic.

When you spot a hazard ahead and need to slow or stop, warn the drivers behind you in three ways. Turn on your flashers. Tap your brakes lightly three or four times, which flashes your brake lights. And use a hand signal while you slow and stop. Together these tell drivers behind you that something is wrong ahead before they reach it. A hazard you can see may be hidden from the driver behind you, so the more clearly you warn them, the more time they have to slow down. Use all three warnings, not just one. Each warning adds to the others.

lines.text: If not, stop where you are seen.

narration.text: If your vehicle has trouble, start the stop with your flashers, or with your turn signals if the vehicle has no flashers. Pull fully off the road, clear of traffic. When getting fully clear is impossible, stop where drivers behind you can see both the car and the driver, and never stop just past a hill crest or a curve, where approaching drivers cannot see you in time. Then call for roadside rescue and wait inside the vehicle until it comes. So the sequence is warn behind, clear the road or park visibly, and then wait inside for rescue.

lines.text: Trap: any shoulder spot is fine.
Truth: never just past a crest or curve.

narration.text: Here is a trap. When a car starts to fail, drivers often stop at the first place they can, even if it is just past a curve or over the top of a hill. That is exactly where drivers behind cannot see you until it is too late. When you cannot get fully off the road, stop where drivers behind can see the car and the driver, never just past a hill crest or curve. A second trap is getting out to walk for help. The handbook says to call for roadside rescue and wait inside the vehicle until it arrives. Being seen is the whole point of the rule.

Here is a quick check: your car has trouble and you cannot get fully off the road. Where should you avoid stopping? Make your choice. The answer is just past a hill crest or a curve. When getting fully clear is impossible, stop where drivers behind can see the car and the driver. A spot just past a crest or curve hides you from approaching traffic. If you named the crest and the curve, you have the visibility rule. Then, once stopped, turn on your flashers, call for roadside rescue, and wait inside the vehicle. Stay inside until help arrives.

lines.text: Clear the road, be seen, wait inside.

narration.text: To finish this section, when you see a hazard ahead, warn drivers behind you with flashers, three or four light brake taps, and a hand signal while slowing and stopping. When your own vehicle has trouble, start with your flashers, or turn signals if there are no flashers, and pull fully off the road clear of traffic. If that is impossible, stop where drivers behind can see car and driver, never just past a hill crest or curve. Then call for roadside rescue and wait inside the vehicle. That completes the introduction to driving basics.
